tur58-0: Brief dizziness that starts when lying down, turning over or looking up: what is BPPV, which canal is affected, how is the Epley manoeuvre done, does it go away on its own, and when should you seek urgent help? Step-by-step drawings, the evidence and a short history.
tur58-1: A spinning sensation that starts suddenly when lying down in bed, turning over in bed or looking up, and usually lasts less than a minute, is mostly caused by small crystals in the inner ear moving out of place. It is the most common cause of inner-ear dizziness and often improves with a simple head manoeuvre.
tur58-2: People whose dizziness went away completely with the Epley manoeuvre; 21% with a sham manoeuvre or no treatment
tur58-5: In the most common, posterior canal type, the diagnosis is made with the Dix-Hallpike test: a physician or physiotherapist turns your head to a certain angle, lies you back quickly and watches for a characteristic movement of your eyes. The test also shows which ear is affected. The American Academy of Otolaryngology guideline recommends against routine MRI or CT scans in patients who meet the diagnostic criteria.
tur58-6: Treatment is with repositioning manoeuvres that move the crystals out of the canal and back to where they belong; the best known is the Epley manoeuvre. In a Cochrane review covering 11 studies and 745 patients, in the five studies making this comparison (273 patients) dizziness went away completely in 56% of those given the Epley manoeuvre and 21% of those given a sham manoeuvre or no treatment; no serious side effects were seen. In one study in the review (81 patients), a single Epley manoeuvre was more effective than Brandt-Daroff exercises done three times a day for a week.
tur58-8: According to the guideline, in about 85–95% of BPPV cases the crystals are in the posterior canal; in about 5–15% the horizontal (lateral) canal is affected. Which canal is affected determines the manoeuvre to be used.
tur58-11: Recognised with the Dix-Hallpike test, which the guideline describes as the gold standard for diagnosis. Treatment uses repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley or Semont. The Epley steps on this page are for the posterior canal.
tur58-14: If the history fits BPPV but the Dix-Hallpike test shows no eye movement or only horizontal eye movement, it is looked for with the roll test, in which the head is turned quickly 90 degrees to each side while lying on your back. Different manoeuvres (for example the Gufoni) are used for treatment.
tur58-17: 11 studies, 745 patients; in five studies (273 patients) dizziness went away completely in 56% vs 21% (sham manoeuvre or no treatment); no serious side effects were seen.
tur58-19: In one study in the review (81 patients), a single Epley manoeuvre was more effective than Brandt-Daroff exercises done three times a day for a week.
tur58-22: It resolves on its own in about 20% at one month and in up to 50% at three months. The guideline sees observation as an option, but strongly recommends the manoeuvre.
tur58-24: Not recommended for routine use; they do not move the crystals back and can affect balance. Balance exercises (vestibular rehabilitation), on the other hand, are recommended as an option.
tur58-25: From the first description to the Epley manoeuvre
tur58-26: Positional dizziness was described in the early 20th century; the diagnostic test appeared in the 1950s, and the manoeuvres used today in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
tur58-27: Nobel laureate Bárány described dizziness triggered by position after observing it in his own assistant.
tur58-28: Dix and Hallpike described the diagnostic test in a study of 100 patients and were the first to name the condition "benign paroxysmal positional vertigo" (BPPV); the test now bears their names.
tur58-29: Semont and colleagues published the manoeuvre they called "liberatory".
tur58-30: Epley published the repositioning manoeuvre that moves the crystals in the canal back into place; at the time this approach met with harsh criticism.
tur58-31: Self-treatment study (Neurology): 95% of patients who learned to do the Epley manoeuvre at home were free of dizziness within a week.
tur58-32: Cochrane review (11 studies, 745 patients): in five studies (273 patients) dizziness went away completely in 56% with the Epley manoeuvre and 21% with a sham manoeuvre or no treatment.
tur58-33: The American Academy of Otolaryngology updated its guideline: the Dix-Hallpike test for diagnosis and a repositioning manoeuvre for the posterior canal; routine imaging and routine dizziness medicines are not recommended.
tur58-34: In a study of 70 patients who learned to do it themselves, 95% of those doing the Epley manoeuvre at home were free of dizziness within a week. If you have a neck or back condition, a vascular condition or a history of retinal detachment, talk to your physician before doing the manoeuvre.
tur58-35: BPPV can come back. In a study that reviewed 1,012 patients retrospectively in Beijing, the recurrence rate within a year after the manoeuvres was between 23% and 29% depending on age group. If the symptoms are the same, the same manoeuvre usually works again. If it keeps coming back or the symptoms have changed, you need to be reassessed; the guideline recommends reassessment within a month of treatment.
tur58-36: If I do not treat it, will it go away on its own?
tur58-37: It can. According to the guideline, BPPV resolves on its own in about 20% of patients within a month and in up to 50% within three months. The guideline accepts observation as an option for initial treatment in suitable patients; however, the manoeuvre usually brings faster relief. During this waiting period, dizziness can increase the risk of falls, especially in older people.
tur58-38: Usually not. The guideline recommends against routine use of dizziness medicines in BPPV; these medicines do not move the crystals back. If you have severe nausea, ask your physician whether a short course of medicine is needed and which one is suitable.
tur58-39: In these situations, dizziness may be caused not by BPPV but by an emergency such as a stroke.
tur58-41: Dizziness that does not improve within a month despite the manoeuvres, or keeps coming back
tur58-42: Symptoms changing or new symptoms appearing (if any of the emergency signs above are present, call 112 immediately)

tur58-47: Proportion of cases in which non-surgical treatment succeeds
tur58-49: The diagnosis is made by examination; imaging is usually not needed. The examination looks for tenderness over the bony bump on the inner side of the elbow. Bending the wrist against resistance and turning the forearm inwards against resistance increase the pain; stretching the wrist backwards with the elbow straight can also be painful.
tur58-50: An X-ray may be requested if symptoms do not settle or another problem is suspected. MRI and ultrasound can show changes in the tendon but are not needed for the diagnosis. Because irritation of the ulnar nerve, which runs along the inner side of the elbow, can accompany up to 60% of cases, the nerve is also assessed in the examination.
tur58-51: Golfer's elbow makes up less than a fifth of tendon pain on the inner and outer sides of the elbow; most cases are tennis elbow on the outer side.
tur58-52: If you need a painkiller, ask your physician which one is suitable.
tur58-53: Golfer's elbow has been studied less than tennis elbow; much of the evidence guiding treatment is carried over from tennis elbow studies, and most of the findings below rest on a small number of small studies. Treatment is chosen for the individual.
tur58-56: 5 studies, 143 people: with eccentric exercise, pain decreased and function improved; the benefit was seen particularly when combined with other non-surgical treatments. Superiority over other treatments was shown in only one study; the certainty of the evidence is low.
tur58-58: May give short-term relief (less than 12 weeks); in the long term, results are worse than with other injections and recurrence is more frequent. No benefit at one year has been shown compared with observation and physiotherapy.
tur58-61: In a small retrospective, non-randomised study published in 2022 (55 people, most with tennis elbow), pain and function at 6, 12 and 24 months were better in those given PRP injections than in those who continued physiotherapy; the proportion needing surgery was 0% vs 20%. Evidence for golfer's elbow is very limited.
tur58-62: Rarely needed. It may be considered for severe symptoms that have not responded to 6 months of non-surgical treatment, or symptoms lasting more than 12 months.
tur58-64: Rest your forearm on the table. Start with the back of your hand on the table, then turn it so your palm faces down; hold for 5 seconds and slowly return. When it becomes easy, hold a tin can.
tur58-66: From the CommonSpirit Houston and Rehab Science YouTube channels. The videos are in English; in the player you can choose Settings → Subtitles → Auto-translate and pick your language.
tur58-67: A video from a healthcare organisation (CommonSpirit Houston) showing exercises you can do at home.
tur58-68: Both are pain from overuse of the tendons attached to the elbow; the difference is the location. In golfer's elbow, the pain is on the inner side of the elbow and the muscles that bend the wrist and fingers are affected. In tennis elbow, the pain is on the outer side and the muscles that bend the wrist backwards (extend it) are affected.
tur58-69: An elbow strap worn on the forearm (epicondylitis brace) may give relief by reducing pressure on the painful spot. According to StatPearls, the strap may help more than physiotherapy in the first 6 weeks, but by week 26 there is no difference. It is used together with reducing load and exercise.
tur58-70: Without treatment, symptoms can last between 6 months and 2 years. Non-surgical treatment succeeds in more than 95% of cases. Modifying the activities that increase pain for at least 6 weeks is recommended; load modification and treatment usually take 6–12 weeks in total.
tur58-71: I have numbness in my ring and little fingers; is it related?
tur58-72: It may be. Irritation of the ulnar nerve, which runs along the inner side of the elbow, can accompany golfer's elbow in up to 60% of people. In this case, the nerve should also be examined during the assessment. If the numbness does not go away or you have weakness in your hand, see a physician.
tur58-73: Golfer's elbow has been studied less than tennis elbow. In a 2026 systematic review of five studies covering 143 people, exercises that work the muscle while it lengthens (eccentric) reduced pain and improved function; the benefit was reported to be seen particularly when combined with other non-surgical treatments. However, the studies were few and small, and the certainty of the evidence is low. According to an NHS leaflet, with the right exercises and small changes in activity most people get better in 8–12 weeks; if the pain has lasted for months, recovery may take longer. Complete rest is not recommended; it is important to keep moving the elbow gently.
